cases.q: Teen hit the side of his head, lucid for an hour, now drowsy.
cases.why: Lens-shaped (biconvex) bright blood pressed against the skull: an epidural hematoma. It can't cross the suture lines because the dura is stuck there. Usually arterial (middle meningeal artery under a temporal bone fracture). Treatment: emergency craniotomy and evacuation.

cr.t: Epidurales Haematom.jpg (a red arrow was digitally removed)

cases.q: Older adult on blood thinners fell a few days ago, now confused.
cases.why: A crescent that follows the curve of the brain and can cross sutures: a subdural hematoma from torn bridging veins. Fresh blood is bright, older blood turns grey then dark. Big or symptomatic ones are drained (burr holes or craniotomy).

cases.dx: Intracerebral hemorrhage spreading into the ventricles
cases.q: Sudden headache and collapse in a man with very high blood pressure.
cases.why: A big intracerebral hemorrhage that has broken into the ventricular system (blood layering in the ventricles). Blood in the ventricles can block CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus, which may need an external ventricular drain.

cases.q: Headaches, vomiting in the morning and blurry vision for weeks.
cases.why: Ballooned ventricles with squashed sulci: hydrocephalus (too much CSF under pressure). Atrophy also makes big ventricles, but then the sulci are big too. Treatment is draining CSF: a shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

cases.q: Weeks of worsening headache and new weakness on one side (MRI with contrast).
cases.why: Thick irregular ring of enhancement around a dead (necrotic) centre inside the brain: classic glioblastoma, the most common malignant primary brain tumour in adults. Main mimic: abscess (check DWI). Treatment: maximal safe surgical resection, then radiotherapy plus an alkylating chemotherapy drug (temozolomide class).

cases.q: Sudden weakness of the left arm and face, started 10 hours ago.
cases.why: Dead, swollen brain holds extra water, so it looks darker (hypodense) on CT, in the shape of an arterial territory (here the middle cerebral artery). In the first hours a CT is often still normal: it's done mainly to exclude bleeding before clot-busting treatment.

cases.q: Stroke with left-sided weakness AND loss of part of the visual field.
cases.why: Dark tissue over the lateral hemisphere (middle cerebral artery) AND the occipital lobe (posterior cerebral artery). Some people's PCA branches off the internal carotid (fetal PCA), so one carotid blockage can hit both.

cr.t: Right MCA and PCA territories infarct.jpg

cases.q: 'Worst headache of my life', came on like a thunderclap.
cases.why: Bright blood filling the CSF spaces around the base of the brain (basal cisterns) and in the fissures: subarachnoid hemorrhage, most often from a ruptured aneurysm. Next step: CT angiogram to find it, then coiling or clipping.

cr.a: Dr. George Jallo, pediatric neurosurgeon at Johns Hopkins
